The library is quiet the following morning. Professor Stone is again at the central desk, working through a ledger beneath a pair of shaded lamps.

You ask, “Which publicly available records describe the human seat’s last active years? I’d like to look at the original records if they’re open to students.”

Stone’s pen stops. His eyes move briefly from your face to the Garvey signet before he closes the ledger.

“The open collection contains official abstracts, published addresses, and an index of petitions submitted by the final human delegation.” His answer becomes more formal than it was when he helped you find the Council primer. “The original correspondence, working drafts, and unabridged committee minutes are restricted. Students require the chancellor’s signature for each requested collection.”

He indicates a tall glass-fronted cabinet beneath the gallery. Its brass lock bears the Academy seal.

“The public index is still useful. It records documents excluded from the abstracts, even when it cannot give you their contents.”

Stone leads you to the historical shelves and removes three volumes. The first is a set of official Council summaries from the final decade before the human collapse. The second is titled *Petitions and Arbitrations of the Human Delegation: A Public Index*. The third contains selected speeches by Dan Garvey, identified in its frontispiece as the last active human Council representative.

“The summaries omit failed motions and most private deliberation,” Stone says. “Use the index beside them. A missing text may still have a date, submitting office, and subject.”

He places the books on an open reading table.

“If you decide to request an original, the catalogue entry will give you its collection number. The access form is held in the chancellor’s office.”

Stone returns to his desk. Before reopening his ledger, he aligns the same small stack of catalogue cards twice. The three public volumes remain available before you.
